clinicalScope: Haemoglobin as the oxygen‑carrying protein in red blood cells, focusing on its biochemistry, genetics and clinical relevance for adult patients in East African low‑resource hospitals.
title: Haemoglobin Biochemistry and Clinical Correlates
subject: Biochemistry & genetics
summary: Haemoglobin is the iron‑containing protein that transports oxygen and carbon dioxide in red blood cells. Understanding its structure, synthesis, and disorders helps clinicians diagnose anaemia, polycythaemia and haemoglobinopathies, especially where laboratory resources are limited.

sections.p: Haemoglobin (Hb) is a tetrameric metalloprotein in erythrocytes that binds up to four O₂ molecules, delivering oxygen to tissues and returning CO₂ to the lungs.
b: Each Hb molecule consists of two α‑ and two β‑globin chains (HbA) in adults.
The iron atom in the heme group reversibly binds O₂; affinity is modulated by pH, CO₂, temperature and 2,3‑BPG (Bohr effect).
Carbamino‑Hb and bicarbonate transport account for most CO₂ carriage.
Normal adult Hb concentration: 120–160 g/L (women) and 130–170 g/L (men).

sections.p: The globin chains are encoded by genes on chromosomes 11 (α‑globin) and 16 (β‑globin). Heme synthesis occurs partly in mitochondria and partly in the cytosol of erythroid precursors.
b: α‑globin genes: HBA1, HBA2; β‑globin gene: HBB.
Heme biosynthesis steps: ALA → porphobilinogen → ... → protoporphyrin IX + Fe²⁺ → heme.
2,3‑BPG binds the β‑chains, lowering O₂ affinity and facilitating release in tissues.
Post‑translational modifications (e.g., acetylation) fine‑tune function.

sections.h: Pathway or mechanism step by step
sections.p: Oxygen loading in the pulmonary capillaries and unloading in peripheral tissues follow cooperative binding, described by the sigmoid oxygen‑dissociation curve.
b: Step 1: O₂ enters alveoli, diffuses into blood, binds deoxy‑Hb (Hb + 4 O₂ → HbO₂).
Step 2: 2,3‑BPG stabilises the T‑state, shifting the curve right in hypoxia.
Step 3: In tissues, increased CO₂, H⁺, temperature promote O₂ release (Bohr effect).
Step 4: CO₂ is carried as carbamino‑Hb (≈5 %) and as bicarbonate (≈70 %).

sections.p: Key enzymes drive heme synthesis; iron, vitamin B6, B12 and folate are essential cofactors for globin production.
b: δ‑Aminolevulinic acid synthase (ALAS) – rate‑limiting, requires pyridoxine (B6).
Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase – deficiency causes porphyria cutanea tarda.
Ferrochelatase inserts Fe²⁺ into protoporphyrin IX; iron deficiency reduces Hb output.
Erythropoietin (EPO) from kidney stimulates red cell production.

sections.p: Hb synthesis is tightly coordinated with erythropoiesis and iron homeostasis.
b: Hypoxia → ↑EPO → marrow erythroid proliferation.
Hepcidin, produced by liver, blocks ferroportin; inflammation raises hepcidin → functional iron deficiency.
Feedback: high Hb/hematocrit suppresses EPO.
Genetic regulation: locus control region (LCR) upstream of α‑globin cluster.

sections.p: Adequate Hb ensures tissue oxygen delivery for aerobic metabolism; low Hb forces reliance on anaerobic glycolysis, causing lactate accumulation.
b: Cardiac output rises to compensate for anaemia (high‑output failure risk).
In chronic hypoxia, 2,3‑BPG rises, shifting O₂ curve right.
Iron deficiency impairs mitochondrial respiration via reduced cytochrome function.
Severe anaemia (<70 g/L) can precipitate tissue hypoxia despite normal cardiac output.

sections.p: Disorders of Hb synthesis or structure manifest as anaemia, polycythaemia, or haemoglobinopathies, each with distinct epidemiology in East Africa.
b: Iron‑deficiency anaemia – most common; diet low in heme iron, chronic malaria or helminthic blood loss.
Sickle cell disease (HbS) – β‑globin point mutation (Glu6Val); prevalent in malaria‑endemic zones.
β‑Thalassaemia trait – reduced β‑chain synthesis; common in coastal Kenya and Tanzania.
Polycythaemia vera – clonal myeloproliferation; rare but important when Hb > 180 g/L.

sections.p: When electrophoresis is unavailable, sickling test or solubility test can screen for HbS.

t.b: What is the haemoglobin concentration and red cell indices? → Low Hb with low MCV suggests iron deficiency; high MCV with high HbA₂ suggests β‑thalassaemia trait.
What morphological clues are present? → Microcytosis, hypochromia (iron deficiency); target cells (thalassaemia); sickled cells (SCD).
Is iron store depleted? → Ferritin < 30 µg/L confirms iron deficiency; acute phase reaction may raise ferritin falsely.
Which Hb fractions are present? → ↑HbS in SCD; ↑HbA₂ (>3.5 %) in β‑thalassaemia trait.
Is marrow response appropriate? → Elevated retics in haemolysis; low in aplastic states.

sections.p: Key pathologies linked to abnormal haemoglobin affect oxygen delivery, cause hemolysis or hyperviscosity.
b: Anaemia → fatigue, dyspnoea, tachycardia; severe (<70 g/L) may cause heart failure.
Sickle cell crisis → vaso‑occlusion, acute chest syndrome, splenic sequestration.
Thalassaemia major → severe anaemia, skeletal deformities, iron overload from transfusions.
Polycythaemia → hyperviscosity, headache, thrombosis risk.

sections.p: Management targets the underlying cause, corrects Hb level, and prevents complications.
b: Iron deficiency – oral ferrous sulfate (or IV iron if malabsorption); treat helminthic infection.
Sickle cell – hydroxyurea to raise HbF, prophylactic penicillin, vaccination, transfusion for severe crises.
β‑Thalassaemia trait – usually no treatment; counsel on carrier status.
Polycythaemia vera – phlebotomy to keep haematocrit < 45 % and low‑dose aspirin.

sections.p: Pitfalls often arise from mis‑interpreting laboratory values or overlooking local disease patterns.
b: Ferritin may be normal or high in infection, masking iron deficiency.
Relying on Hb alone can miss early thalassaemia (normal Hb, abnormal indices).
Assuming all anaemia is nutritional ignores malaria‑related hemolysis.
Using pulse oximetry alone cannot differentiate between low Hb and low saturation.

sections.p: When faced with a patient with abnormal Hb, follow a systematic framework:
b: 1️⃣ History: diet, menstrual loss, malaria episodes, family history of sickle cell/thalassaemia.
2️⃣ Examination: pallor, jaundice, splenomegaly, tachycardia, blood pressure.
3️⃣ First test: CBC with indices; interpret in context.
4️⃣ Targeted follow‑up: ferritin, smear, electrophoresis as indicated.
5️⃣ Management plan: treat cause, consider transfusion thresholds (Hb < 70 g/L in stable adults).

whenToSeekHelp: Severe dyspnoea or chest pain with Hb < 70 g/L
Acute vaso‑occlusive crisis in sickle cell disease
Signs of high‑output cardiac failure (e.g., pulmonary oedema) in severe anaemia
Sudden neurological change suggesting stroke in sickle cell or polycythaemia

faq.q: Why does 2,3‑BPG shift the oxygen‑dissociation curve?
faq.a: It binds β‑chains, stabilising the low‑affinity T‑state, so O₂ is released more readily to tissues.

faq.q: Can a normal Hb level rule out iron deficiency?
faq.a: No; early iron deficiency may have normal Hb but low ferritin and microcytosis.

faq.q: What is the first‑line test for sickle cell disease in a low‑resource setting?
faq.a: A sickling solubility test; confirm with electrophoresis when available.

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman from rural Tanzania presents with fatigue, pallor and a CBC showing Hb 85 g/L, MCV 68 fL, low ferritin. What is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management? — Iron‑deficiency anaemia; start oral iron, treat any helminth infection, advise dietary iron.

A child with known sickle cell disease develops sudden chest pain and hypoxia. Which investigation is most urgent and why? — Chest X‑ray to assess acute chest syndrome; early antibiotics and transfusion may be needed.
How does chronic malaria infection contribute to anaemia pathophysiologically? — Repeated hemolysis of infected RBCs, dyserythropoiesis, and iron sequestration by hepcidin.
Explain why HbA₂ is elevated in β‑thalassaemia trait and how this helps diagnosis. — Compensatory increase in δ‑chain synthesis raises HbA₂ (>3.5 %); distinguishes trait from iron deficiency.

A patient has Hb 190 g/L, haematocrit 58 %, and no obvious hypoxia. What condition should you consider and what is the first therapeutic step? — Polycythaemia vera; therapeutic phlebotomy to reduce haematocrit below 45 %.
Why might serum ferritin be falsely normal in a patient with concurrent infection? — Ferritin is an acute‑phase reactant and rises with inflammation, masking iron deficiency.

In a low‑resource clinic without electrophoresis, how would you screen for β‑thalassaemia trait? — Look for microcytic hypochromic anemia with normal iron studies; consider family history and target cells on smear.

What is the physiological basis for the Bohr effect and its clinical relevance in sepsis? — Increased CO₂/H⁺ lowers Hb affinity, facilitating O₂ release; in sepsis, this helps tissue oxygenation despite anemia.
When is blood transfusion indicated for anaemia in an adult without cardiac disease? — When Hb < 70 g/L or symptomatic (e.g., severe dyspnoea, tachycardia).
Describe how hydroxyurea benefits patients with sickle cell disease. — Increases fetal Hb (HbF) which inhibits HbS polymerisation, reducing vaso‑occlusive episodes.
